chapters.s: The village had already begun again; and over in the city, once an order of victory has dried completely, its voice no longer sounds like paper. It speaks like dust. The Court of Channa Grove had not been adjourned. It was merely waiting for the next party.
chapters.g: Aruni had opened his old notebook. He had stopped his pen. For many days a desire to write “The End” had been growing inside him. Human beings grow tired and long for an ending. But a village does not want an ending. A village wants a story to become not a burden handed down from generation to generation but work.…

chapters.s: The mind had arrived during the night; now it was the body's turn. At dawn Batuknath Hariharan stood before his cupboard. Before he could answer, Budhba Ghost climbed onto a branch. The air in Channa Grove moved gently. The leaves rustled together, like thousands of pages opening at once. Batuknath Hariharan's journey had not ended.…

Chandrapal Batra would not go to Garh Narikel. He stamped that decision into place on the very morning Batuknath Hariharan was practising the reading of names with Budhba Ghost on a train. And so Chandrapal Batra entered Garh Narikel without going there. His body remained in the city's glass room, but through a crack in the screen his mind hung toward Channa Grove. The inner journey of the rogues had only begun.

The second station in the rogues' inner journey was Raghav. Voice had never mattered in the life of Raghav “Signal” Somani. That morning, in the kabaddi of Channa Grove in Garh Narikel, a new sound arrived. The ghosts asked, “Who has come?” Budhba Ghost cupped his ear. “Not a body. Someone has sent silence.” The Loths smiled. The light of the Raksh grew a little brighter.…

Raghav's silence had already crossed the sea and reached Hong Kong. Lau Kin-Hung never pronounced his full name. It was not the sound of Garh Narikel. It was the sound of his own mind. The mind remained suspended, and a mind that remains suspended will one day drag the body after it.

The minds of all five rogues now hung suspended, and for suspended minds Channa Grove opens its own court. When a person wins in the outer court and loses in the inner one, his gait becomes more measured than before. That morning Budhba Ghost remained awake a little longer in Channa Grove. He turned over a leaf. The next date was written upon it: the night of dreams. He smiled. Human courts give dates so that cases may be postponed.…

The inner court had bound the rogues to waiting. Meanwhile, those whom the court had called defeated rose at dawn without raising a slogan against anyone. The leaves of Channa Grove whispered: 'One who stops fighting and begins working is not merely difficult to defeat - he is impossible to defeat.'

The evening whisper lingered into night. There was no wind in Channa Grove, yet the leaves were moving. And Channa Grove drew its next breath. The story did not stop there. Crocodiles eat bodies, courts eat years, screens eat minds; but when the mind hangs suspended, the story begins again. That night kabaddi did not end - only the next breath was taken.
chapters.g: Raghav's mind retreated. Its erasing breath was spent. It sat in the middle of the court and became silence. Silence had been following him long before this chapter received its name; now silence became his mouth.

chapters.s: The next breath had been drawn. In Channa Grove the first breath of the third kabaddi match had ended, but the game had not. And at that moment the novel moved forward again.

The silence that spread after the fourth breath was not peace. It was the kind of silence in which a river holds back its current to hear who is lying on the bank. And the story of Garh Narikel moved forward again, carrying the fifth breath.
chapters.tu: a bright form of the boatman-Sama-Daun

chapters.s: After the fifth breath, the five drops of water poured at the roots of Channa Grove did not disappear into the earth. They moved within the roots like children’s laughter circling through an old house. All the leaves of Channa Grove moved together. Their movement carried not kabaddi but the sound of a school. The story moved forward—because a name does not tire until it reaches home.

When the name reached home, the seventh breath of the game in Channa Grove began. For six breaths the name had searched for its threshold; in the seventh, the darkness inside that threshold, the smell of rice, the thorn of fear and the dimmed lamp of dream slowly began to open. In Garh Narikel the children set out for school. Ananya turned and looked back toward Channa Grove. The leaves were moving—not with kabaddi, but with the rustle of homework.…

The seventh breath travelled on in the children's pockets as three pebbles—home, fear, dream. All day the pebbles kept rattling: at school, on the field ridge, after the mobile screen had gone dark, and at night beneath the pillow. Thus the eighth breath ended—without forgiveness, without punishment, but with recognition of beginnings. The story moved forward because a door had opened into the rogues' inner worlds. No one changes the instant a door opens; but air enters.…

After the eighth breath, the game in Garh Narikel stopped for two days. The children found this astonishing, because the ghosts' kabaddi never stopped. Thus the ninth breath did not end; it became practice. Far away in their rooms, the rogues kept reading names—wrongly, then correctly, then stumbling again. In Garh Narikel, the victims kept hearing their names. The children kept asking questions.…
